meta.resolution_basis: The local comparison ends by contrasting the laboratory’s observed responses: firearms identification and drug crystal testing continued without the proposed reforms, whereas toxicologists began reporting calculated uncertainty (pp. 624, 628, 632–633, Table 2). This closes the observed local practices, not the continuing nationwide disputes.
meta.fieldwork_scale: The primary ethnography [8 words of Bechky (2020), p. 612] at Metropolitan County Crime Lab [6 words of Bechky (2020), p. 612]. The researcher observed four units—DNA/forensic biology, firearms, toxicology, and controlled substances—spending [6 words of Bechky (2020), p. 614] for approximately three days per week. Observation included every analyst and supervisor in those units, laboratory meetings, occasional courtroom activity, and eight training sessions for justice-system audiences. Near the end, the researcher conducted semi-structured interviews with some analysts, every unit supervisor, and the lab director and deputy director. Visits beyond the main site included three other laboratories in the same state, with an interview with each director, and a one-day visit to an eastern U.S. county laboratory, with an interview of its deputy director and observations of three units. The researcher attended three professional gatherings lasting three, two, and one day, respectively, and examined the 2009 National Academy of Sciences report. The methods section does not give a numeric interview total or observation-hour total (pp. 612–615).

claims.statement: When one field occupation gains legitimacy from a new technology, comparisons with its work can induce changes among nearby occupations that never use that technology.
claims.outcome: Alteration of neighboring occupations’ work practices
claims.asserted_direction: When another occupation’s technology becomes a recognized point of comparison, neighboring nonusers have more impetus to alter their work.

claims.statement: Treating forensic DNA as an especially credible form of evidence placed the scientific standing of other forensic occupations under greater examination.
claims.outcome: External scrutiny of non-DNA forensic disciplines
claims.asserted_direction: When DNA profiling was singled out as exemplary, scrutiny of other forensic practices increased.

claims.statement: Workers are more receptive to changes presented through occupational comparisons when those changes accord with what they consider good work.
claims.outcome: Willingness to revise work practices
claims.asserted_direction: When a proposed change agrees with occupational values, willingness to adopt it is higher; when it offends those values, willingness is lower.

claims.statement: The fit between existing methods of producing evidence and the proposed model affects how readily workers can reshape their own procedures.
claims.outcome: Ease of adapting occupational techniques
claims.asserted_direction: When existing procedures can accommodate the desired form of evidence, adaptation is easier; where the methods cannot be reconciled, it is harder.

claims.statement: The institutional settings in which an occupational group encounters comparisons help determine which aspects of technological legitimacy it notices and how it responds.
claims.notes: The paper specifies different kinds of institutional routes and responses but no single positive or negative direction across all routes; hence no outcome or asserted direction.

claims.statement: New technologies can reorganize occupational jurisdictions, job content, resources and workplace relationships, whether by establishing new roles or unsettling existing ones.
claims.notes: General endorsed synthesis of existing technology-adoption research (including Abbott and Barley); the described movements are multidirectional, with no single outcome polarity.

claims.statement: The local history, work relations and politics in a setting shape how an introduced technology is put to use, so the same device need not have identical organizational effects.
claims.notes: Author-endorsed synthesis of cited empirical studies, including Barley; it asserts contextual conditioning but no signed outcome.

claims.statement: Higher professional authority gives an occupational group greater scope to oppose technological changes that would reshape its tasks.
claims.outcome: Capacity to resist imposed task changes
claims.asserted_direction: When a group commands more occupational authority, it is better positioned to resist changes to its tasks.
claims.notes: Qualified theoretical generalization drawing on earlier workplace studies; this is not offered as the forensic cases’ main explanation.

claims.statement: Using a technology that audiences regard as advanced can enhance an occupation’s reputation for being modern and worthy of trust.
claims.outcome: Perceived legitimacy of a technology-using occupation
claims.asserted_direction: When an occupation adopts a technology audiences associate with progress, its perceived legitimacy tends to rise.
claims.notes: The theoretical argument is advanced with citations to symbolic-technology studies and occupational examples.

claims.statement: Occupational communities help reproduce the practices and standards of conduct of their members through shared activity and ties to professional bodies.
claims.notes: Author-endorsed synthesis of earlier studies of professional communities; no one outcome is said to rise or fall.

claims.statement: When occupational groups hold incompatible ideas of worthwhile work, cooperation across their boundaries becomes more difficult.
claims.outcome: Collaboration between occupational groups
claims.asserted_direction: When occupational values conflict more sharply, cross-group collaboration declines.
claims.notes: Endorsed finding from prior literature, with the engineers-and-marketers study used as an example.

claims.statement: Forensic scientists must fashion evidence that meets the expectations of scientific and legal audiences at the same time.
claims.notes: Setting-level characterization of the profession and its audiences, not a directional relationship.

claims.statement: Observing organizational life directly helps disclose workers’ local interpretations of institution-level expectations and their responses to them.
claims.outcome: Visibility of workers’ interpretations and responses
claims.asserted_direction: When researchers observe people in their work setting, locally situated interpretations and responses become more observable.
claims.notes: Methodological rationale endorsing the cited ethnographic perspective, not a result about forensic occupational change.

claims.statement: The national report’s favorable comparison of DNA with other forensic methods heightened non-DNA analysts’ concern that their approaches would have to be revised.
claims.outcome: Perceived need to revise evidentiary work
claims.asserted_direction: When the report exempted DNA from its broad scientific criticism, non-DNA analysts felt more pressure to reconsider their practices.

claims.statement: DNA operated as a benchmark in forensic science despite the absence of a field-wide official rule requiring others to mimic it.
claims.notes: The contrast between informal evaluation and formal standard-setting is descriptive, not an outcome movement.

claims.statement: The different techniques bundled into DNA profiling let other forensic groups select different features as the basis for judging their own practices.
claims.notes: The paper identifies occupation-specific points of comparison, but does not assert a monotonic direction for which feature is chosen.

claims.statement: DNA reports’ numerical population comparisons, error accounting and durable graphs gave outsiders stronger grounds to treat the evidence as impersonal and scientifically secure.
claims.outcome: Perceived scientific objectivity of DNA evidence
claims.asserted_direction: As DNA reporting adds reviewable numerical and graphical representations, outside perceptions of its objectivity become stronger.

claims.statement: DNA analysis still depends on case-by-case judgment, collaborative interpretation and efforts to cope with imperfect samples, despite its tidy public-facing results.
claims.notes: Describes the discrepancy between laboratory practice and outside perceptions without saying that an outcome increases or decreases.

claims.statement: The higher standing of forensic biology was accompanied by disproportionate access to laboratory funding, equipment and personnel compared with neighboring units.
claims.outcome: Resources available to forensic biology
claims.asserted_direction: When DNA profiling enjoys a more privileged position, the DNA group receives more relative resources.
claims.notes: The resource disparity is attributed to the unit members’ observations; the precise allocation process is not documented here.

claims.statement: The greater attention and resources given to forensic DNA generated ill feeling among specialists whose work received less recognition.
claims.outcome: Resentment among other forensic specialties
claims.asserted_direction: When DNA receives preferential attention and resources, resentment in the other specialties rises.

claims.statement: Even with comparable scientific degrees, differing evidence methods and relationships with the justice system fostered distinguishable occupational cultures within the laboratory.
claims.outcome: Differences among the occupational cultures
claims.asserted_direction: When work techniques and ties to legal institutions differ more across units, their occupational cultures become more distinct.

claims.statement: Scientific and media criticism, together with admissibility disputes elsewhere, led firearms specialists to worry about the standing of their evidentiary method.
claims.outcome: Firearms examiners’ concern about evidentiary legitimacy
claims.asserted_direction: When public criticisms and courtroom disputes intensify, firearms examiners become more concerned about the admissibility and standing of their evidence.

claims.statement: Creating detailed images and comparing conclusions through colleague review strengthened the support firearms examiners could offer for their identifications in court.
claims.outcome: Documentary support for firearms identification testimony
claims.asserted_direction: When examiners compile clearer images and review them together, their identification conclusions acquire stronger documentary support.
claims.notes: Describes the purpose the paper assigns to records and review, not an independently measured change in courtroom outcomes.

claims.statement: Valuing seasoned, overall pattern recognition made the local firearms examiners reluctant to rely on a numerical rule for counting similar marks.
claims.outcome: Routine use of CMS in firearms identifications
claims.asserted_direction: When examiners place greater trust in their holistic expert assessments, their use of CMS as a routine decision rule is lower.

claims.statement: The absence of a usable firearms counterpart to DNA population statistics limited examiners’ ability to convert bullet-mark assessments into percentage-based conclusions.
claims.outcome: Use of population-statistical firearms identifications
claims.asserted_direction: When firearms comparison lacks a defensible DNA-style population basis, the ability to adopt percentage-based firearms reporting is lower.

claims.statement: The proximity and urgency of the encounter with evaluation affected whether occupational members had reason to negotiate changes in their everyday work.
claims.outcome: Likelihood of local practice change
claims.asserted_direction: When evaluative pressure is immediate and personally encountered in local settings, a practice change becomes more likely than under distant criticism.

claims.statement: The prospect of a near-term challenge to local toxicology testimony prompted the unit to begin reporting a calculated range of measurement uncertainty.
claims.outcome: Use of quantified uncertainty in toxicology reports
claims.asserted_direction: When an impending local court challenge targets missing uncertainty estimates, the unit introduces quantitative uncertainty reporting.

claims.statement: Earlier accreditation-driven planning and the unit’s existing records made it quicker to implement the uncertainty calculations when the court challenge arose.
claims.outcome: Speed of implementation of measurement-uncertainty reporting
claims.asserted_direction: When a unit already has relevant accreditation plans and measurement records, it can introduce uncertainty estimates sooner.

claims.statement: The toxicologists welcomed uncertainty estimates partly because using numerical checks to avoid mistakes aligned with their established standards of careful, traceable work.
claims.outcome: Approval of new error-reporting procedures
claims.asserted_direction: When uncertainty reporting affirms a group’s established concern with preventing errors, approval of the new reporting is stronger.

claims.statement: Debates in the narcotics professional community, sharpened after the national review, made laboratory drug analysts fear they might lose permission to use crystal-based tests.
claims.outcome: Anxiety over continued acceptance of crystal testing
claims.asserted_direction: When professional debate shifts toward instrumented testing, concern that crystal testing could be prohibited increases.

claims.statement: GC/MS produced permanent machine records more similar to DNA outputs, and this conferred comparative legitimacy on it even though the field also regarded crystal identification as scientifically sound.
claims.outcome: Perceived legitimacy of instrument-based drug identification
claims.asserted_direction: When an identification method generates DNA-like machine records, its perceived suitability as the preferred scientific method is higher.

claims.statement: For the local narcotics unit, high caseloads, rapid deadlines and limited instrument capacity made relying entirely on GC/MS impractical compared with rapid crystal tests.
claims.outcome: Ability to finish narcotics cases by their deadlines
claims.asserted_direction: When analysts must rely on slow GC/MS runs with too few instruments, their ability to meet required case turnaround falls.

claims.statement: The threatened replacement of crystal testing with standardized machine runs met resistance because narcotics analysts prized variety, discretionary judgment and hands-on chemistry.
claims.outcome: Willingness to switch from crystal tests to routine GC/MS
claims.asserted_direction: When a switch threatens craft expertise, independence and varied work, narcotics analysts are less willing to adopt routine GC/MS.

claims.statement: Technical feasibility does not ensure occupational acceptance: a group may reject a workable substitute when it conflicts with the kind of work its members want to do.
claims.outcome: Acceptance of technically feasible work changes
claims.asserted_direction: When an otherwise practicable alternative violates occupational values, acceptance of that alternative falls.
claims.notes: This interaction condition is distinguished from the separate general value-fit and technique-fit relationships in C03 and C04.

claims.statement: Immediate, local challenges supply more occasions for occupational members to interpret institutional demands together and organize practical responses.
claims.outcome: Opportunities for local discussion and action about evaluation
claims.asserted_direction: When evaluative challenges arrive directly in the local workplace or courtroom, opportunities for collective interpretation and action increase.

claims.statement: Occupations sharing evaluators or other interested audiences may be more exposed to comparisons originating in each other’s technological practices.
claims.outcome: Reach of evaluative spillovers across occupations
claims.asserted_direction: When occupations have more audiences and concerns in common, evaluative pressure is more likely to extend between them.
claims.notes: Presented as a possible way to define the reach of spillover; the paper explicitly says this single-field study cannot settle the boundary.

claims.statement: Occupational principles about worthwhile work arise in part from the particular technical tasks people perform, and those principles are used to assess proposed changes.
claims.notes: The paper expressly treats occupational technique and values as analytically separable but entwined in daily practice; it does not identify a fixed signed outcome.

claims.statement: Pressure on sociological ethnographers to make research more transparent is likely to meet resistance because identifying participants would undermine valued anonymity practices and the comparison arrives through relatively distant public discussion.
claims.outcome: Adoption of source-identifying research transparency by ethnographers
claims.asserted_direction: When public pressure for disclosure conflicts with established confidentiality commitments and lacks immediate local force, uptake of source-identifying transparency is lower.
claims.notes: Explicit prediction outside the observed forensic setting, supported by the author’s discussion of a published professional debate; not a finding from the fieldwork.

claims.statement: As digital technologies spread across types of expert work, benchmarking occupations against their new users may extend into a greater range of industries.
claims.outcome: Number of occupational fields subject to evaluative spillovers
claims.asserted_direction: As digital technologies become more prevalent across industries, evaluative spillovers are expected to occur across more occupational fields.
claims.notes: Forward-looking extrapolation based on examples the paper cites, not an observed trend measured in this ethnography.

contrast_pairs.episode_a: Firearms specialists at the main laboratory kept their judgment routines despite outside criticism.
contrast_pairs.episode_b: Toxicologists at the same laboratory accelerated numerical uncertainty reporting under an impending local legal challenge.
contrast_pairs.held_comparable: Both groups worked in MCCL and had to defend forensic results before legal audiences while being compared with DNA evidence.
contrast_pairs.differs_in: A distant admissibility dispute produced no new local firearms practice; an approaching challenge to the local toxicology result coincided with adopted uncertainty reporting.
contrast_pairs.basis: The paper contrasts the absence of local firearms challenges and retained routines with the pending local toxicology dispute and implemented reporting measures (pp. 624–628, 633–635).

contrast_pairs.episode_a: The main laboratory’s narcotics analysts kept using rapid crystal identification rather than make routine use of compatible machine tests.
contrast_pairs.episode_b: Its toxicologists incorporated additional numerical information into reports based on compatible instrumental chemistry.
contrast_pairs.held_comparable: Both occupations had access to instrumental analysis that could be related to the DNA model, and both were assessed through broader professional standards.
contrast_pairs.differs_in: Narcotics valued discretionary varied bench work and retained crystals; toxicology valued control of error and introduced uncertainty calculations.
contrast_pairs.basis: The table and discussion report method compatibility for both groups, contrasting drug-unit retention of crystal testing with toxicology’s new reporting (pp. 632–633, 637).

contrast_pairs.episode_a: Toxicology first prepared a longer-term plan to estimate measurement uncertainty for accreditation.
contrast_pairs.episode_b: The same unit brought forward the uncertainty calculations when warned of an impending courtroom dispute.
contrast_pairs.held_comparable: Both episodes concern the same unit and the same type of measurement-uncertainty reporting.
contrast_pairs.differs_in: A prospective multi-year plan became an immediate reporting project in response to an upcoming case.
contrast_pairs.basis: The paper places the prior accreditation plan before the court threat, then reports implementation as the court date approached (pp. 627–628).

contrast_pairs.episode_a: Firearms examiners prepared clearer images and shared technical reviews to better justify expert identification decisions.
contrast_pairs.episode_b: The same occupation rarely relied on a numerical consecutive-mark rule despite its availability and clarity to outsiders.
contrast_pairs.held_comparable: Both were ways for MCCL firearms examiners to make a judgment about matching marks understandable and defensible to third parties.
contrast_pairs.differs_in: Documentary images and peer review were used; numerical matching criteria were rarely used.
contrast_pairs.basis: The consecutive firearms technique and values sections juxtapose routine imaging and shared review with seldom-used numerical mark counting (pp. 621–623).

contrast_pairs.episode_a: Eastern drug laboratories frequently made instrumental mass-spectrometric identification their primary option.
contrast_pairs.episode_b: Western laboratories, including MCCL, commonly used microscopic crystal formation for familiar substances.
contrast_pairs.held_comparable: Both sets of laboratories identified controlled substances within the same forensic specialty, and the paper identifies both analytical methods as scientifically accepted.
contrast_pairs.differs_in: The two regions favored different methods with different forms of lasting records and different processing times.
contrast_pairs.basis: The paper explicitly contrasts the eastern preference for GC/MS with the western preference for crystals and describes the different outputs (pp. 628–630).

declared_gaps.statement: The evidence comes principally from one laboratory in one occupational field, so this analysis establishes the possibility of cross-occupation comparison rather than how it would unfold in other fields.
The research cannot fix a general boundary for which other occupations count as neighbors that could be affected by comparisons; it leaves the reach of the process for future investigation.
The author attended talks by firearms examiners working elsewhere but did not obtain evidence about those speakers’ actual practices back in their own laboratories.

absences.evidence_class: Disposition of the anticipated local toxicology courtroom challenge
absences.basis: The paper describes the impending defense challenge and accelerated uncertainty calculations but does not give the final hearing result or trial disposition (pp. 625, 627–628).
